title: Parts of speech
note: Traditional grammar sorts words into eight parts of speech: nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections. A word's part of speech depends on the job it does in a given sentence, so the same word can be a noun in one sentence and a verb in the next.

read.title: Words at work
text: Many learners memorize the parts of speech as if each word wore a permanent label. In fact, English assigns a word its part of speech by the job it does in a particular sentence. Take the word light. In "Turn on the light," it names a thing, so it is a noun. In "Light the candles," it expresses an action, so it is a verb. In "She packed a light bag," it describes a noun, so it is an adjective.

The same test settles harder cases. The word before can be a preposition ("before dinner"), a subordinating conjunction ("before we eat"), or an adverb ("I have seen this before"). To decide, look at what follows it. A preposition takes a noun or pronoun as its object. A subordinating conjunction introduces a whole clause with its own subject and verb. An adverb stands on its own.
This habit pays off later. Comma rules, agreement and pronoun case all depend on seeing what each word is doing. When a sentence puzzles you, ask of each word: what is its job here?
